#### 5.3.6 How reviews and CI treat stacked PRs

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [G1] Reviewers see only the diff of their own layer (stack map in the merge box). GitHub's "Rebase stack" retains approvals when the layer's diff is unchanged even with "dismiss stale approvals" on (GitHub docs). With hand-built stacks and Graphite, rebasing the lower layer re-triggers approval dismissal, so Graphite requires the setting off and pullnotifier.com advises disabling it to avoid re-review cascades; pullnotifier.com also advises reviewing bottom-to-top and marking upper PRs as drafts.
**Source:** https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/get-started/about-stacked-prs ; https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-06-stacked-pull-requests-generally-available ; https://pullnotifier.com/tools/stacked-prs ; https://graphite.com/docs/github-configuration-guidelines. Reliability: official docs plus vendor blogs.
**Relevance:** HIGH
**Relationship to codebase:** extends (web-03 G1) the sequence-and-gates inputs: a stack is a way to land a multi-piece unified review panel in dependency order while each piece is reviewed alone, and the lower piece gates the upper under GitHub's bottom-up merge rule. Whether the repo's review bots (Augment, Codex) review against the stack base or `master` is not verified.

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [G2] CI: GitHub docs say CI checks triggered by PRs on the default branch run for all PRs in the stack, and branch protection is evaluated against the stack base, not the immediate parent. CircleCI blog: each PR in a stack needs its own validation; updating a lower PR and rebasing those above re-runs pipelines across the stack (four branches can mean four sets of builds); it suggests path filtering, and says that if managing the stack costs more than reviewing one larger PR, keep the change together. diffox.ai reports that for hand-built chains checks "did not run again" after a rebase and the old commit's result was displayed (single-source, unverified). NOT verified: whether GitHub Actions `pull_request` workflows with a `branches:` filter match the PR's BASE branch, so a hand-built stacked PR whose base is another feature branch would not trigger a workflow filtered to `master`/`integration` (only a Stack Overflow snippet hinted at this: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/79292495/trigger-action-on-pull-request-not-working). A 404 on GitHub's "Optimizing CI for stacked pull requests" page meant GitHub's own advice could not be read.
**Source:** https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/get-started/about-stacked-prs ; https://circleci.com/blog/stacked-prs-and-ci ; https://diffox.ai/blog/github-stacked-pull-requests. Reliability: official docs; CircleCI vendor blog.
**Relevance:** MEDIUM
**Relationship to codebase:** extends (web-03 G2). The codebase's CI workflow triggers are the source of truth; compare them with the above in research item 2.18 / CI findings.

**Source conflicts flagged in web-03 (G3):**

| Claim | Source | Conflicting source | Web-03 resolution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Squash-merge cannot be used on intermediate PRs; GitHub's native merge queue does not handle dependent PR ordering | pullnotifier.com (blog, undated "(2026)" title) | GitHub GA docs (D1): stacks support merge commit, squash and rebase and are merge-queue aware | Blog treated as superseded for native GitHub stacks, still valid for hand-built chains and some third-party tools; prefer the docs |
| Squash or rebase default merge settings break stack identity tracking | AlphaSignal (preview-period blog, D2c) | GitHub GA docs (D1) | Prefer the docs; test before relying on either |

### 5.4 Finding schemas and review bots

Source file: `research/web-04-finding-schemas-review-bots.md` (its section numbers are cited as "web-04 N.N"). Codebase context handed to the web researcher and not re-verified there: the review package has two finding contracts (v1 anchor quotes plus a category set; v2 path:line citations plus an optional lens); `src/superclaude/pr_submit/` has its own severity router and third-party reviewers (Augment, Codex); a future PR-code-review module needs a file-and-line location type. Augment's review output format was not researched (no official source found): a gap.

#### 5.4.1 SARIF 2.1.0

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 1.1] A SARIF `result` carries `ruleId`, `message`, `locations[]`, optional `relatedLocations[]`, `kind`, `level`, `fingerprints`, `partialFingerprints`, `guid`, `correlationGuid`, `baselineState`. `kind` (evaluation state, spec 3.27.9: `notApplicable`, `pass`, `fail`, `review`, `open`, `informational`) and `level` (how bad: `error`, `warning`, `note`) are separate properties. Identity: `guid` identifies the result in one run; `correlationGuid` the equivalence class of logically identical results across runs; `fingerprints` are full stable identities; `partialFingerprints` contribute to identity and are expected to change when surrounding code changes; `baselineState` is `new`, `unchanged`, `updated` or `absent`. Location: `locations[].physicalLocation.artifactLocation.uri` (+ optional `uriBaseId` such as SRCROOT) and `region` (`startLine`, `startColumn`, `endLine`, `endColumn`); per spec 3.29.4, if `region` is absent the physicalLocation refers to the entire artifact (file-level finding).
**Source:** https://sarif.info/Result (secondary explainer, well-maintained) ; https://docs.oasis-open.org/sarif/sarif/v2.1.0/sarif-v2.1.0.html (OASIS SARIF 2.1.0 Plus Errata 01, official standard).
**Relevance:** HIGH
**Relationship to codebase:** extends (web-04 1.1). The v2 path:line citation maps to `artifactLocation.uri` + `region.startLine`; the v1 anchor-quote location has no SARIF-native analogue. SARIF separates state (`kind`/`baselineState`) from severity (`level`), matching a panel that needs both severity and verdict/resolution state on one finding.

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 1.2] GitHub code scanning consumes a SARIF subset. Example: `tool.driver.rules[]` with `id`, and rule `properties` keys `kind` (e.g. `path-problem`), `problem.severity` and `security-severity` (numeric string such as `9.8`); results carry `ruleId`, `message.text`, `locations[].physicalLocation` with `artifactLocation.uri` and `region.startLine/startColumn/endColumn`, and `partialFingerprints` with `primaryLocationLineHash` (example `39fa2ee980eb94b0:1`) and `primaryLocationStartColumnFingerprint`. `relatedLocations[]` carry an `id`, location and message. Producer guidance: relative URIs with `uriBaseId: "%SRCROOT%"`.
**Source:** https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/code-scanning/sarif-files/sarif-support (official GitHub docs).
**Relevance:** HIGH
**Relationship to codebase:** extends (web-04 1.2). A minimal interoperable location is (relative path, start line, optional end line, optional column), and the dedup fingerprint is a hash of line content plus an occurrence counter, not the line number. The v1 anchor quote is conceptually a content-based fingerprint that survives line drift; a bare path:line citation does not.

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 1.3] The SARIF spec calls for stable fingerprints and has an appendix on fingerprint properties (deterministic computation; incorporate tool name, rule ID and physical location of the target). Vulnerability-management needs (new/unchanged/fixed state, approved suppression, remediation validation) are representable but consumers must still apply them in context; partial fingerprints exist to follow findings through code motion.
**Source:** https://boostsecurity.io/blog/sarif-cant-save-you-now (vendor blog).
**Relevance:** MEDIUM
**Relationship to codebase:** supports (web-04 1.3) keeping finding state across review rounds (ledger) as a layer on top of the finding record rather than inside it.

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 1.4] GitLab ingestion: requires `ruleId` and a physical location (findings without either are not added); severity defaults to `medium` when unset; finding identity = report type + fingerprint of `ruleId` + location fingerprint of the form `file:startLine:endLine`; results in the same file with the same `ruleId` and no `region` collapse into one finding and the rest are silently discarded.
**Source:** https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/detect/sarif (official GitLab docs).
**Relevance:** MEDIUM
**Relationship to codebase:** extends (web-04 1.4) with a pitfall: if a unified finding record lets `location` be file-only, or lets `category` stand in for a rule id, a downstream consumer can silently dedup distinct findings. Suggests requiring a line (or content anchor) plus a category/rule id on every record meant to be exported.

#### 5.4.2 reviewdog rdjson

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 2.1] rdjson top level: `source {name, url}`, `severity` (default for the set), `diagnostics[]`; rdjsonl is one diagnostic per line. Diagnostic: `message`, `location {path, range {start {line, column}, end {line, column}}}` (end optional), `severity` (`ERROR`/`WARNING`/`INFO`), `code {value, url}`, `suggestions[] {range, text}`. Stated purpose: a generic protocol between diagnostic tools and development tools (editors, reviewdog, code review APIs), with multiline ranged comments, severity, rule code with URL and code suggestions; suggestions are applied only by reporters that support them (github-pr-review, gitlab-mr-discussion, local). reviewdog reporters include `github-pr-review`, `github-pr-check`, `github-annotations`/`github-pr-annotations` and `local`.
**Source:** https://github.com/reviewdog/reviewdog/blob/master/proto/rdf/README.md ; https://github.com/reviewdog/reviewdog (official repository documentation, well-maintained).
**Relevance:** HIGH
**Relationship to codebase:** extends (web-04 2.1). rdjson is the closest existing format to a PR-review finding (path, range, severity, rule code, optional suggested fix) with no confidence, dedup or resolution fields. A shared finding record projectable into rdjson (message, path, line range, severity, code=category) would let a future PR-code-review module reuse reviewdog reporters. Its three-level severity maps one-to-one onto SARIF `error/warning/note`.

#### 5.4.3 GitHub pull-request review comment API

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 3.1] `POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}/comments` takes `body`, `commit_id`, `path`, `line`, `side` (`LEFT`/`RIGHT`), optional `start_line` and `start_side`; `position` (lines down from the first `@@` hunk header) is described as "closing down"; 422 on validation failure or if spammed; triggers notifications and can hit secondary rate limits. `POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}/reviews` takes `commit_id` (not the latest SHA may render comments outdated), `body`, `event`, and `comments[]` each with `path` (required), `body` (required), and `position` or `line`/`side`/`start_line`/`start_side`.
**Source:** https://docs.github.com/rest/pulls/comments ; https://docs.github.com/rest/pulls/reviews (official GitHub REST docs).
**Relevance:** HIGH
**Relationship to codebase:** extends (web-04 3.1). The location type a PR-code-review module needs is `(path, line, side, optional start_line/start_side, commit_id)`. `commit_id` is required context that the v1 anchor and v2 path:line contracts do not appear to carry (not verified against the code): without a commit SHA a line citation is not reproducible against a moving PR head.

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 3.2] User-reported constraints (not official statements): the create-review endpoint returns comment objects in the older position/diff_hunk shape with `line`/`side` null (re-fetching by id returns the line model); one report of a direct single-comment `gh api` call with `start_line`/`start_side`/`line`/`side` returning 422 while the same comment inside a review `comments[]` array worked; comments on lines outside the diff hunks are rejected with 422 `pull_request_review_thread.line is not part of the diff`, although the web UI allows commenting on unchanged lines of changed files (announced Sept 2025) and API support was reported as limited; no API (REST or GraphQL) to append comments to an existing pending review; file-level comments cannot be mixed with line comments inside one review via REST (Oct 2024 answer).
**Source:** https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/202426 ; https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/13358 ; https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/187218 ; https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/168380 ; https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/143197 (community discussions and issues, lowest tier).
**Relevance:** MEDIUM (forum reports; verify against the current API)
**Relationship to codebase:** extends and constrains (web-04 3.2). A PR-code-review module cannot post a finding whose line is outside the diff, so the finding record needs a "postable versus report-only" distinction (outside the diff degrades to the review body or a file-level comment). The existing fork-only `pr_submit` flow is unaffected (a posting-time constraint).

#### 5.4.4 Severity models in code scanning and review bots

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 4.1] GitHub code scanning has two severity ideas. All alerts have a level of Error, Warning or Note; security alerts additionally carry a security severity Critical/High/Medium/Low derived from a numeric `security-severity` score (0.1-3.9 low, 4.0-6.9 medium, 7.0-8.9 high, 9.0-10.0 critical; 0.0 none; following CVSS), shown in preference to level. PR check failure defaults: security-severity critical or high fails the check; for non-security alerts severity `error` fails; both thresholds are configurable (repository settings or rulesets: "Errors", "Errors and Warnings", "All"; security "High or higher", "Medium or higher", "All").
**Source:** https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/code-scanning/code-scanning-alerts ; https://github.blog/changelog/2021-07-19-codeql-code-scanning-new-severity-levels-for-security-alerts (official); https://safeguard.sh/resources/blog/sarif-security-severity-how-github-maps-scores-to-levels (blog, secondary).
**Relevance:** HIGH
**Relationship to codebase:** extends (web-04 4.1). The standard pattern for a severity router: a coarse 3-level result severity plus an optional finer score, with a configurable gate threshold decoupled from the finding. It parallels the `pr_submit` severity router (fixes confirmed findings of Medium or higher; lower ones only reported, per the repo CLAUDE.md as cited by web-04): the threshold should be configuration over a shared ordinal scale, not a property of the finding record.

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 4.2] CodeRabbit labels a finding with four independent closed vocabularies, explicitly "not one severity ladder": Type (Nitpick, Potential issue, Refactor suggestion); Severity (ranked critical, major, minor, trivial; plus `info` and `none` outside the ranking); Category (six areas: functional correctness, security and privacy, data integrity and integration, performance and scalability, stability and availability, maintainability and code quality); Effort (cost to fix). Overview items carry a priority band p1-p4. Acceptance rate is computed per severity and category as accepted comments / posted comments, where "accepted" means CodeRabbit can verify the feedback was addressed.
**Source:** https://docs.coderabbit.ai/change-stack/findings ; https://docs.coderabbit.ai/guides/code-review-overview ; https://docs.coderabbit.ai/guides/dashboard-metrics (official vendor docs).
**Relevance:** HIGH
**Relationship to codebase:** supports (web-04 4.2). The v1 contract's category set and the v2 contract's optional lens are both "what area" axes; this model confirms severity and category must stay orthogonal and a lens/category is a label, not a filter or a severity. The acceptance-rate metric is resolution-derived and needs a per-finding resolution state in the ledger.

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 4.3] Greptile assigns a 0-5 confidence score per pull request (5 production ready ... 0-1 critical problems), computed from severity and quantity of issues, change complexity and alignment with codebase patterns; inline comments carry severity levels and suggested fixes; a configurable severity threshold filters noise. The vendor states the score is a triage tool, not a rubber stamp. Vendor statistics are vendor-reported.
**Source:** https://www.greptile.com/docs/code-review/first-pr-review ; https://www.greptile.com/agent (official vendor docs) ; https://www.greptile.com/what-is-ai-code-review (vendor marketing).
**Relevance:** MEDIUM
**Relationship to codebase:** extends (web-04 4.3). For the rf-qa replacement ("checklist-and-confidence model") bot practice puts confidence at the unit-of-review level (PR/document verdict), not per finding; per-finding confidence is not in SARIF or rdjson. Web-04 suggests the finding record stays confidence-free (or carries an optional field) and the verdict record carries confidence.

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 4.4] One evaluation reports GitHub Copilot review surfacing new comments on re-run that did not relate to the latest changes (unstable finding set across runs), and Greptile placing some findings only in the summary rather than inline. Precision and recall figures in a comparison (e.g. Greptile 66.2% precision, Copilot 56.5%) are vendor-reported benchmarks and unverified.
**Source:** https://t2informatik.de/en/blog/how-effective-are-ai-code-reviews (blog) ; https://www.morphllm.com/comparisons/greptile-vs-copilot (vendor comparison).
**Relevance:** LOW
**Relationship to codebase:** supports (web-04 4.4) the need for a stable finding identity (dedup key) across review rounds in the ledger; does not contradict any code finding.

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 4.5] Codex review (a third-party reviewer already used by `pr_submit`): official docs say Codex on GitHub posts a standard GitHub review and flags only P0 and P1 issues, with a `[P1]` title tag plus explanation; repository guidance comes from `AGENTS.md`. A gist reproducing the review prompt defines P0 (drop everything), P1 (urgent), P2 (normal), P3 (low), asks for short line ranges (avoid over 5-10 lines), a numeric `priority` 0-3 (null if unknown) and an "overall correctness" verdict that ignores non-blocking issues. Issue 27691 (user report): when Codex finds an issue it creates a formal `COMMENTED` PullRequestReview with a full `commit_id` and inline comments; when it finds nothing it posts only an issue comment (short SHA in prose) and a reaction, so a clean result cannot be bound to the exact PR head SHA. A third-party action (`gersmann/codex-review-action`) skips findings whose line is not in the current diff and on re-runs does semantic dedup against prior unresolved comments, reporting new and still-relevant prior findings separately.
**Source:** https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/third-party/github (official OpenAI docs) ; https://gist.github.com/cbh123/ce4893a10ed2b87a89d9114b08118a08 (secondary copy of codex-rs/core/review_prompt.md; the prompt may have changed) ; https://www.cubic.dev/blog/codex-code-review ; https://www.qodo.ai/glossary/what-is-codex-code-review (competitor blogs) ; https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/27691 (issue on the official repo).
**Relevance:** HIGH
**Relationship to codebase:** extends and partly contradicts an assumption (web-04 4.5). Codex uses a 4-step P0-P3 ordinal and shows only P0/P1 on GitHub, CodeRabbit uses critical/major/minor/trivial/info, SARIF uses error/warning/note, so the in-repo `pr_submit` severity router must normalise at least three vendor vocabularies (and Augment's, not researched) onto one internal ordinal; a unified record's `severity` should be that ordinal with the vendor label kept as an opaque string. The "overall correctness verdict" is a verdict-level record separate from findings, matching the planned cluster/verdict/ledger split. The clean-result-has-no-SHA gap is a reason for the ledger to record the reviewed head SHA itself.

#### 5.4.5 Resolution, suppression and dedup vocabularies

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 5.1] Resolved state lives on the review thread, not the comment. User-reported (no official GraphQL reference page was fetched): resolving a conversation uses the GraphQL mutations `resolveReviewThread` and `unresolveReviewThread` with a thread node id (`PRRT_...`) from `reviewThreads.nodes[].id`; `isResolved` is a thread field; replies use `addPullRequestReviewThreadReply`; REST does not return thread node ids. Reports say a Copilot coding agent's `GITHUB_TOKEN` could not call `resolveReviewThread` and that Copilot re-review leaves earlier comments behind (feature request to mark them outdated or dismiss).
**Source:** https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/12419 ; https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/19206 ; https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/196714 ; https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/187953 (forum-level).
**Relevance:** MEDIUM
**Relationship to codebase:** extends (web-04 5.1) and matches the CLAUDE.md description of `/sc:pr-submit` (replies to and resolves review comments it fixed): the unit of resolution is a thread id, so a ledger row for a PR finding needs a `thread_id` (and comment id) in addition to path and line.

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 5.2] GitHub code scanning alert state is `open` or `dismissed`; `dismissed_reason` is required when dismissed and is one of `false positive`, `won't fix`, `used in tests`, `mitigated` (or null); `dismissed_comment` is free text. The alert response shows `rule {id, severity, tags, description}`, `tool {name, guid, version}`, and `most_recent_instance {ref, commit_sha, message, location {path, ...}}`, so an alert is a rule-level object with per-commit instances.
**Source:** https://docs.github.com/rest/code-scanning/code-scanning (official GitHub REST docs).
**Relevance:** MEDIUM
**Relationship to codebase:** extends (web-04 5.2). A small closed resolution vocabulary with a mandatory reason when closing without a fix is a model for the ledger's disposition field (for example fixed, rejected as false positive, accepted as won't-fix). The alert/instance split mirrors the cluster/finding split in the planned shared core.

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 5.3] A SARIF `suppression` object has a `kind` (`inSource`, a syntactic construct in the code, or `external`; only `inSource` text was seen) and, per the standard's rationale, `suppressions` is either null for all results or non-null for all results in a run. `baselineState` records state against a previous run (`new`, `unchanged`, `updated`, `absent`). Per the standard, `kind` defaults to `fail` and any `level` other than `none` requires kind `fail`. The `dismiss-alerts` action maps SARIF suppressions to GitHub alerts by rule id + file + line + column and dismisses with reason `won't fix` and comment `Suppressed via SARIF`.
**Source:** https://docs.oasis-open.org/sarif/sarif/v2.1.0/sarif-v2.1.0.html (official standard) ; https://github.com/advanced-security/dismiss-alerts (GitHub-maintained action repository).
**Relevance:** MEDIUM
**Relationship to codebase:** extends (web-04 5.3). Suppression is a property of the result and cross-run state is a separate property; the planned ledger can adopt the same split (decision with who/why, state versus previous round). The identity key used by interop tooling is rule id + file + line + column, again an argument for a location with a line and an id-like category on every exported finding.

**Finding:** [EXTERNAL] [web-04 5.4] Cross-round dedup and carry-forward in bots: a third-party action passes prior unresolved comments to the model so it avoids reposting them, then asks separately which prior comments are still relevant, reports new and still-relevant counts separately, and deletes its own prior summary comment on each run. A blog evaluation observed Copilot re-runs surfacing comments unrelated to the latest changes.
**Source:** https://github.com/marketplace/actions/codex-code-review-actor (third-party GitHub Marketplace listing; not official) ; https://t2informatik.de/en/blog/how-effective-are-ai-code-reviews (blog).
**Relevance:** MEDIUM
**Relationship to codebase:** supports (web-04 5.4) adding a per-finding `status` across rounds (new, carried, resolved, superseded) in the ledger rather than treating each round as a fresh finding list.

**Minimal interoperable finding record (web-04 section 6; a synthesis by the web researcher from sections 1 to 5, not a quoted standard):**

| Field | Evidence for needing it | Web-04 section |
|---|---|---|
| stable id (rule/category id plus per-finding id) | SARIF `ruleId`, `guid`; rdjson `code.value`; GitLab and GitHub require a rule id to ingest or dedup | 1.1, 1.4, 2.1 |
| location: repo-relative path, start line, optional end line, optional column | SARIF `region`; rdjson `range`; PR API `path`/`line`/`start_line` | 1.2, 2.1, 3.1 |
| location side and commit SHA (only for PR posting) | PR API `side`, `commit_id`; Codex issue about SHA binding | 3.1, 4.5 |
| content anchor or fingerprint (survives line drift) | SARIF `partialFingerprints.primaryLocationLineHash`; v1 anchor quote | 1.2 |
| message | present in every format | 1.1, 2.1, 3.1 |
| severity as a small ordinal (3-4 levels) plus optional vendor label | SARIF `level`; rdjson ERROR/WARNING/INFO; Codex P0-P3; CodeRabbit 4+2 levels | 2.1, 4.1, 4.2, 4.5 |
| category/lens kept separate from severity | CodeRabbit four independent axes; SARIF rule tags | 4.2 |
| tool/reviewer identity | SARIF `tool.driver`; rdjson `source`; alert `tool` | 1.2, 2.1, 5.2 |
| optional suggested fix | rdjson `suggestions`; GitHub suggestion blocks | 2.1 |
| state/disposition outside the finding (ledger): status versus baseline, dismissal reason, thread id | SARIF `baselineState`/`suppressions`; code scanning `dismissed_reason`; GraphQL thread id | 5.1, 5.2, 5.3 |
| confidence at verdict level, not per finding | Greptile PR-level 0-5 score; Codex overall correctness verdict; no per-finding confidence in SARIF or rdjson | 4.3, 4.5 |

Web-04 reports not found in any source: a standard per-finding confidence field, and a standard "quote anchor" location type; both are the project's own extensions (the v1 anchor quote is closest to SARIF `region.snippet` plus a fingerprint, but `snippet` was not verified).

**Vocabulary comparison (web-04 4.1, 4.2, 4.5, 2.1, 1.1):**

| Source | Severity vocabulary | Gate or display note |
|---|---|---|
| SARIF / code scanning `level` | error, warning, note (and none) | Numeric `security-severity` 0.1-10.0 maps to low/medium/high/critical; gate is a configurable threshold |
| reviewdog rdjson | ERROR, WARNING, INFO | Maps one-to-one onto SARIF levels |
| CodeRabbit | critical, major, minor, trivial (plus info, none); p1-p4 on overview items | Severity, category, type, effort are independent axes |
| Codex on GitHub | P0, P1, P2, P3 (numeric priority 0-3) | Only P0 and P1 shown on GitHub |
| Greptile | per-PR confidence 0-5; inline severity levels | Configurable severity threshold |
| Augment | not researched | Gap (web-04 section 7) |

**Web-04 caveats (section 7):** GitHub PR API behaviours in 5.4.3 (web-04 3.2) and 5.4.5 (web-04 5.1) come from forum or issue reports, not official docs, and the API changes (the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` header appears in current official examples), so re-verify before design depends on them. Vendor statistics are vendor-reported and not used as design evidence. The SARIF `level` value `none` and the `kind` value list were read from the OASIS text and sarif.info; the full `suppression.kind` and `baselineState` tables were only partly visible.

### 5.5 External Research Summary

#### Key takeaways (external context only)

| # | Takeaway | Subsection | Relevance | Relationship to codebase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Judge biases (position, verbosity, self-preference) are documented; standard remedies are order swapping or randomisation, ground-truth grounding and not letting a model judge its own family's output. Verbosity bias appears much smaller in recent judges. [SOURCE WITHDRAWN: arXiv 2606.19544, withdrawn by arXiv Admin, v2 2026-11-03; figure not used] | 5.1.1, 5.1.5 | HIGH | supports E2 blind judging; extends | <!-- Source: Base (original, modified) — M-24 item 2: withdrawn source -->
| 2 | Cross-family panels beat a single large judge on QA-style tasks (B1), but errors stay correlated across providers (B2) and 9 judges from 7 families gave about 2 independent votes (B3). Transfer to code review is `[UNVERIFIED]`. | 5.1.2 | HIGH | supports and partly contradicts the independent-opinions assumption |
| 3 | Independent review plus aggregation is a sound default; debate adds little over voting on benchmark tasks. | 5.1.3 | HIGH | supports E2 independent-then-merge |
| 4 | For code review, aggregating several independent reviews raises recall (SWR-Bench F1 up to +43.67%) because reviewers and runs flag largely different change-points. | 5.1.4 | HIGH | supports union merge |
| 5 | Merge and verdict rules in use are opposed (union, 2-of-3 majority that discards single-reviewer findings, unanimity, any-pass); no study compares them on findings with ground truth. | 5.1.4, 5.1.7 | HIGH | extends; design choice not settled by external sources |
| 6 | Agreement must be reported chance-corrected; judge stability across reruns is not correctness. | 5.1.5 | HIGH | extends E1/E2 measurement |
| 7 | Cheap non-LLM verification (mechanical citation check) separated hallucinated from genuine citations on one sample; a passing citation proves existence in context, not correctness. A union of automated reviewers still falls well short of human review (c-CRAB 41.5%). | 5.1.6, 5.1.4 | HIGH / MEDIUM | supports citation verification; limits replacement claims |
| 8 | `PostToolUse` fires only on success; hooks load in `claude -p` unless `--bare`; `--bare` drops hooks even when passed via `--settings`. | 5.2.1, 5.2.2 | HIGH | extends E2 `[UNVERIFIED]` assumption |
| 9 | Field reports: `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, `SessionStart` command hooks worked in print mode; `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit` and prompt-type hooks were unreliable or unsupported. | 5.2.8 | HIGH / MEDIUM | supports (partly) and cautions |

#### Statement on precedence

External findings in this section supplement and never override code-verified facts. All findings are external context drawn only from the four web research files, each flagged by its own reliability tier. Where a web finding conflicts with a code-verified fact, the code wins and the discrepancy is stated; none of the four web files recorded such a conflict, and web-03 explicitly defers to research item 2.18. Codebase statements quoted in the web files were supplied as context, not verified by the web researchers, and are labelled `[UNVERIFIED]` where those files said so.

#### R1 5.1 Multi-reviewer panel aggregation

Source file: `research/web-01-panel-aggregation.md` (Tavily; sections 1, 3 and 4 of that file). The jury-versus-single-judge and judge-bias material of web-01 section 2 is reported in 5.3 because it concerns who judges.

##### R1 5.1.1 Aggregation rules and measured error rates

| Finding | Source | Date | Relevance | Relationship to codebase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Union voting ("any reviewer flags") in a zero-shot multi-agent vulnerability ensemble gave 82.7% recall, 48.8% precision and 85.0% false-positive rate; weighted voting gave 37.7% recall with 35.3% false-positive rate. Authors call 85% FPR the main deployment constraint and unsuitable for CI gating. | https://arxiv.org/html/2602.17875v1 (MultiVer; preprint) `[S]`; exact numbers MEDIUM confidence until extracted | Feb 2026 | HIGH | supports. The ledger rule "row blocking = any member blocking" (R1-C1, research/02) maximises recall at the cost of precision; direction matches the measured 65 versus 38 blocking result (research/05). Domain is vulnerability classification, so direction transfers, magnitude does not. |
| Cross-judge majority voting (self-judge excluded) reduces leniency but treats all judges as equally reliable; calibrated weighted majority voting weights each vote by an online estimate of that judge's error rates from inter-judge agreement and tracked an oracle within 0.5 percentage points in simulation. | https://arxiv.org/html/2609.12002v1 (preprint) `[E]` | Sep 2026 (arXiv id) | HIGH | extends. Our `confidence` field is a count of distinct reviewers that no decision reads (R1-C1; research/02 R1-D4: displayed, not decision-bearing). Evidence for the weighted rule is simulation-only: an option, not a proven rule. |
| Self-aggregation of the same LLM over several runs (Self-Agg, n=10, Gemini-2.5-Flash) raised F1 to 21.91% (+43.67%) and recall to 30.44% (+118.83%); the gain is mostly recall and absolute F1 stays low. A secondary summary says F1 plateaus near 5-10 runs. | https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01494 (SWR-Bench; preprint) `[S]`; plateau claim https://zylos.ai/research/2026-03-01-multi-model-ai-code-review-convergence `[2]` | Sep 2025; secondary 2026-03-01 | MEDIUM | extends. Aggregation does not evidence that false blockers go away; a blocking gate on raw aggregated findings would over-block. |
| Fourteen LLM validators had true-positive rate above 96% but true-negative rate typically below 25% (they confirm and rarely reject). Majority vote "is not good enough". A minority veto (mark invalid if at least 4 of 14 say so) gave the lowest maximum error: 2.8% after data repair, TPR 95.5%, TNR 30.9%; the n=4 threshold itself needed a human-labelled calibration set. Minority veto was robust to missing votes; a super-majority rule that defaults a missing vote to "invalid" did slightly worse. A regression bias model on a small labelled set reached 1.2% maximum absolute error. | https://arxiv.org/html/2510.11822v2 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11822 (OpenReview https://openreview.net/forum?id=3IsAoRHi9n; preprint) `[E]` | Oct 2025 | HIGH | extends and partly cautions. Reverse polarity of our ledger (there one reviewer can assert blocking, R1-C1). Shows a lenient grader is a weak precision filter, so the blind grader (R1-C5) needs a measured true-negative rate. The "missing vote counted as an answer" shape is R1-D2/R1-D3 (an invalid reviewer counted as no finding, R1-C3). Task is feedback validity, so transfer is by analogy. |
| In requirement-conformance checks LLMs over-reject correct code; asking them to explain and propose a fix raised misjudgment. A reviewer can be right for the wrong reason: GPT-4o symptom-level match 98.2% on HumanEval versus bug-cause match 59.1%. | https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00539v1 `[E]`; journal version https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10515-026-00638-5 | Mar 2026; journal 2026 | HIGH | supports. Direction of the measured wrong-blocker problem (65 versus 38, research/05). Suggests a cause-level evidence check (our citation and anchor checks) is worth more than another reviewer's opinion. Benchmarks are small coding sets, not spec review. |

##### R1 5.1.2 Multi-agent review systems in production

| Finding | Source | Date | Relevance | Relationship to codebase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cursor Bugbot early pipeline: eight parallel passes with randomised diff order, bucket similar bugs, majority vote to drop bugs seen in one pass, merge buckets, filter categories, validator model for false positives, dedupe against bugs already posted. Largest later gains came from a fully agentic redesign; whether majority voting survived is not stated `[U]`. Resolution rate 52% to 70% is a secondary, self-reported figure and is a resolution-by-merge metric, not a false-positive rate. | https://cursor.com/blog/building-bugbot `[V][E]`; secondary https://victorinollc.com/thinking/ai-code-review-bugbot, https://www.spotdev.co.uk/blog/cursor-bugbot-ai-code-review `[2]` | Date not shown (refs "this fall"); secondary 2026 | HIGH | extends. Dedupe against earlier runs is the same job as our cross-round row matching (research/02, ledger.py:166-171). Bugbot passes are one model with shuffled input, so a singleton there is more likely noise than in a heterogeneous panel (web-01 inference, see 5.1.4). |
| Cloudflare: up to seven specialised reviewers in parallel; a coordinator deduplicates, re-categorises and applies a reasonableness filter (reads source when unsure). Approval is a fixed rubric: any critical item or production safety risk gives "significant concerns" and blocks; several warnings revoke approval; one warning in a clean change still gets "approved with comments". Bias toward approval is stated explicitly. | https://blog.cloudflare.com/ai-code-review `[V][E]` | Date not shown | HIGH | supports. A single adjudicator, not the reviewers, decides blocking from a severity rubric after a verification filter; reflect's blocking classes Drift and Regression (R1-C4, research/05) are the same pattern. Differs: a single warning never blocks there. Our ledger states no verdict bias. |
| LinkedIn: each subagent (a distinct model-and-harness pairing) reviews the full diff blind to the others; a finding raised by two or more is elevated as high-confidence; a one-model finding is not discarded but sent for verification and rated separately. | https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/ai/high-signal-ai-code-review-that-adapts-to-your-codebase-at-scale `[V][E]` | Date not shown | HIGH | supports using overlap (our `confidence` overlap versus single, display-only per R1-C1) as a routing input to verification, not a drop rule and not ignored. contradicts the Bugbot-style drop-singletons rule for heterogeneous panels. |
| 294 human-confirmed defects over 33 artifacts, fifteen model versions from eight providers: no large-sample model exceeded about 61% code recall; 56.8% (167 of 294) of confirmed defects were found by exactly one model; median pairwise cross-family Jaccard about 0.29; coverage rose from about 47% (one reviewer) to about 72% (two), with diminishing returns after. Authors recommend two or three independent reviewers plus a human verifying against source. | https://zenodo.org/records/21328807 (self-published, single team corpus) `[A]` | Reviews dated Apr-Jul 2026 | HIGH (reliability LOW to MEDIUM) | supports keeping a union-of-reviewers candidate set (R1-C1 recall) and contradicts a hard quorum as the only blocking gate: requiring agreement would have dropped more than half the confirmed defects in this corpus. Also supports reflect degrading a single-reviewer merge (R1-C4, contract.py:295-296), since the second reviewer adds the most. |
| Ensembles are mostly run for recall and false positives stack with each reviewer; the cost of a false positive depends on whether a human or an agent reads it next. A figure of 93.4% unique issues with no same-line overlap across four parallel reviewers is second-hand and unverified. | https://dev.to/pyor/multiple-ai-code-reviewers-do-parallel-bots-help-57ag `[2][U]`; https://www.augmentcode.com/guides/deep-code-review-recall-vs-precision `[V]` | Aug (year not shown); guide updated Aug 2026 | MEDIUM (reliability LOW) | extends. Supports a two-stage design (wide candidate set, then verification) over a stronger vote at the first stage. |
| Mozilla.ai Star Chamber: several providers with no cross-visibility; issues classed consensus (all), majority (two or more) or individual (one provider, "may be a specialised insight, or may be noise"); JSON output with typed severity, file:line and category so grouping uses location and category, not fuzzy text. Ellipsis (via ZenML summary): parallel generators then dedup, confidence threshold, a hallucination filter that checks each comment against its evidence, and editing. | https://blog.mozilla.ai/the-star-chamber-multi-llm-consensus-for-code-quality; https://www.zenml.io/llmops-database/building-and-deploying-production-llm-code-review-agents-architecture-and-best-practices `[V]` | Date not shown; Ellipsis 2024 | MEDIUM | supports our typed finding contract and anchor and citation checks as the enabling condition for reliable clustering (research/02 section 1). The Ellipsis evidence filter is the opposite of our rule that a finding whose anchor is absent from the document still becomes an open blocking row (test at tests/review/test_review_ledger.py:408-417, R1-D5). |

##### R1 5.1.4 Within-5.1 conflicts and evidence gaps

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Singleton handling splits the field | Cursor drops findings seen in one pass; LinkedIn verifies them; the Zenodo corpus says most true defects are singletons across families. Web-01 reconciles them by an inference of its own, stated by none of the sources: with homogeneous passes a singleton is likelier noise, with heterogeneous reviewers likelier a real catch. Treat the reconciliation as an unverified hypothesis. Stronger evidence: the Zenodo corpus (measured, but LOW to MEDIUM reliability); Cursor and LinkedIn are first-party design descriptions without error rates. |
| Codebase-side inconsistency noted by web-01 | Reflect degrades a single-reviewer merge (contract.py:295-296) while the ledger passes a round on one valid reviewer (ledger.py:150-157, pinned at tests/review/test_review_ledger.py:385), as recorded in research/02 and research/05. External evidence (Zenodo coverage step, Nine Judges in 5.3) supports treating one reviewer as insufficient for a PASS. Resolution belongs to synth-04. |
| Wording discrepancy | The note that `confidence` is "computed but unused" is only partly true (research/02 R1-D4: displayed, not decision-bearing). External sources treat overlap count as a decision or routing input, so this is a design choice, not a code error. |
| Gap: no measured clustering error | No peer-reviewed measurement of over-merge or under-merge rates when clustering findings from several LLM reviewers, nor of how clustering errors change a blocking verdict. Dedup evidence is practitioner description. |
| Gap: no spec or tasklist panel study | No source evaluated blocking decisions on non-code documents with a panel. |

##### R1 5.1.5 External-research options for the merge and blocking rule (from web-01; options, not decisions)

| # | Option | Basis in 5.1 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Split "candidate" from "blocking": keep a wide any-reviewer candidate set, make a finding blocking only after verification against source (anchor and citation checks first, then an independent adjudicator). This would replace the any-member rule as the decider while keeping it as the candidate filter. | Cloudflare, LinkedIn, Cursor validator, over-rejection study, Zenodo |
| 2 | No hard N-of-M quorum as the only gate; use reviewer overlap to route and prioritise (verify singletons, rank overlaps first); wire the existing display-only `confidence` field into that routing. | Zenodo 56.8% singletons; Nine Judges (5.3) |
| 3 | Treat an invalid or truncated reviewer block as an abstention that counts against the quorum of valid reviewers, not "no findings"; a PASS needs at least two valid reviewers, a FAIL needs one verified blocking finding. Web-01 marks this as its own inference; it would change the assertion at tests/review/test_review_ledger.py:385 on purpose. | Agreeableness study (missing-vote handling), Zenodo second-reviewer step |
| 4 | Tune any vote threshold (for example promoting a verified singleton) on human labels; consider per-reviewer reliability weights only after a calibration set exists (simulation-only evidence). | Agreeableness study; weighted-vote preprint |
| 5 | Dedup on typed fields (location, category, anchor), keep every contributing reviewer id, let the verifier's severity override a reviewer's self-assigned severity, dedupe across rounds; embedding similarity fallback only. | Section 5.1.3 |
| 6 | State the verdict bias explicitly and record per round how many blockers were dropped at verification. | Cloudflare |
| 7 | Measure outcome (share of blocking findings fixed or upheld), not volume; caveat: Cursor's metric is self-reported and is not a false-positive rate. | Cursor |
| 8 | Panel size: three heterogeneous reviewers plus one adjudicator is the evidence-supported size; more needs measured error independence. | Zenodo diminishing returns; Nine Judges |

#### R1 5.2 Severity taxonomies and harmonization

Source file: `research/web-02-severity-harmonization.md` (Tavily). Codebase facts that file marks CODE-VERIFIED (from research/01 and research/10): findings-v1/v2 use three severities (CRITICAL, MAJOR, MINOR) and MINOR can never be blocking, with `blocking` a reviewer-written bool; reflect legacy cards use HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW and card_convert maps `high` to MAJOR plus blocking, and `medium`, `low` and `important` to MINOR non-blocking; rf-qa uses CRITICAL/IMPORTANT/MINOR and blocks "by definition, not by the label"; Auggie and PR review use Critical/High/Medium/Low/Nit with blocking derived from the remapped level; the review-loop prose has a fourth grade "Medium" meaning "any label with blocking false".

##### R1 5.2.3 Cross-tool equivalence and lossless-mapping strategies

Cross-tool equivalence (web-02 section 6.5; documented vendor values, row alignment is the research agent's judgment where no vendor mapping exists):

| Rank | SARIF level | GitHub | Semgrep | SonarQube (legacy / MQR) | CodeRabbit | OWASP | GitLab |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | error (rank high) | critical (over 9.0) | CRITICAL | Blocker | Critical | Critical | Critical (rank 90-100) |
| 2 | error | high (7.0-8.9) | HIGH (= legacy ERROR) | Critical / High | Major | High | High |
| 3 | warning | medium (4.0-6.9) | MEDIUM (= WARNING) | Major / Medium | Minor | Medium | Medium |
| 4 | note | low (0.1-3.9) | LOW (= INFO) | Minor / Low | Trivial | Low | Low |
| 5 | note (rank low) / none | none | none | Info | Info | Note | Info |

Strategies observed (web-02 section 7.2) and what each keeps or risks:

| # | Strategy | Used by | Keeps | Loses or risks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Coarse ordinal plus finer numeric field | SARIF rank, GitLab | Order inside a bucket; a fifth tier above `error` | `rank` has no standard cut points |
| S2 | Severity from impact and likelihood, confidence separate | Semgrep, OWASP, GitHub precision | Why the severity is what it is | Needs two reviewer inputs; none carried today |
| S3 | Obligation separate from severity | Conventional Comments, GitHub gate, Google | Policy changes without re-grading | Free-form obligation can contradict severity (needs a validation rule such as "MINOR cannot block") |
| S4 | Legacy alias table with versioning | Semgrep, SonarQube 10.2 | Old reports keep working | Aliases land mid-scale; Sonar's extreme collapse later called "not ideal" |
| S5 | Native value preserved in a named property | SARIF converter guidance | Exact round trip | Not comparable across tools without a core value |
| S6 | Category-kind-specific scale with a bridge | CodeQL, SonarQube MQR | Each family keeps its natural scale | Two scales to explain; the bridge must carry category |
| S7 | Visibility policy on top of severity | CodeRabbit, GitHub gate | Nothing dropped from storage | Policy lives outside the finding, so exports lose it unless recorded |

Collapse analysis: a 5-to-3 collapse (Critical and High to error, Medium to warning, Low and Nit to note) is not invertible (`error` could be Critical or High; `note` could be Low or Nit); 3-to-5-to-3 is lossless only if the five-level value or `rank` is kept, 5-to-3-to-5 never is. Our PR router has three routes (Critical/High deep fix, Medium fix, Low/Nit report-only; severity_router.py:203-223, research/10), which line up with error/warning/note, so `level` suffices for routing but not for the PR rubric's own Critical versus High distinction (severity-rubric.md:11-61, per web-02).

Where our five vocabularies lose information when mapped to a candidate core (web-02 section 8; the mapping is the research agent's proposal, not stated by any source; full 19-row table in that file):

| Where | Loss | External-research handling |
|---|---|---|
| Review-loop "Medium" (MAJOR label with blocking false) and reflect `MEDIUM` | The medium tier exists only as prose, a card_convert collapse to MINOR, and a PR tier; whether a medium reflect drift blocks is UNDECIDED (an owner decision, not settled by external sources) | Keep `medium` as its own tier; store the native label |
| Reflect deviation classes Authorized expansion and Necessary deviation | Non-defects; forcing a severity inflates counts | Keep as class field with non-defect kind (SARIF `kind` precedent) |
| rf-qa `IMPORTANT` | rf-qa blocks by definition, not label; collides with card_convert `important` to MINOR non-blocking (card_convert.py:82) | Carry `blocking` separately |
| v1 CRITICAL with blocking false | v1 bars only MINOR from blocking (findings.py:100-101) | Keep both fields and flag the contradictory pair |
| Low versus Nit; Critical versus High at `level` layer | Not distinguishable in SARIF `level` | Keep core ordinal or `rank` |
| Codex P0-P3 | Priority, not severity; definitions unverified | Keep as native hint with its own table |

#### R1 5.3 LLM-as-judge and calibration

Source files: `research/web-03-judge-calibration.md` (all sections) and `research/web-01-panel-aggregation.md` section 2 (juries versus single judges). Codebase context recorded in web-03 from research/05 and research/11: reflect requires the calibrator from a different model class than the reviewer; the calibrator agent is written for a 6-dimension troubleshoot rubric while reflect uses 5 dimensions; legacy recorded cards held 0 numeric per-finding calibrations of 689 findings, while shadow runs hold 142 of 142 (research/05 section 5; web-03 line 11 states the shadow figure as 0 of 689, a slip not carried here); the other session scored panels with a blind Opus judge over anonymised merged reports; the E2 judge was blind to reviewer ids but NOT to panel name (research/11 section 2: the judge-one.sh schema contains the combo name, which encodes model names); an experiment grader is blind with a frozen rubric (blocking yes or no); reflect degrades single-reviewer merges and convergence below 0.80 (contract.py).

##### R1 5.3.4 Calibration methods and practice

| Finding | Source | Date | Relevance | Relationship to codebase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Platt scaling suits monotone miscalibration; isotonic regression is non-parametric but overfits small sets (blogs cite roughly 1000+ examples; one study fitted on 60); fit on a calibration split, refit when model, prompt or distribution changes; a blog claim that Platt on 200+ examples cuts ECE 30-60% is marketing-style and excluded. Isotonic reward calibration for judge scores uses a small labelled slice with a fallback for response-length bias. | https://www.kdnuggets.com/a-deep-dive-into-calibration-of-language-models-platt-scaling-isotonic-regression-temperature-scaling; https://futureagi.com/blog/evaluating-llm-confidence-uncertainty-2026 (blogs, LOW); https://arxiv.org/html/2512.11150v1 `[S]` | Dec 2025 (arXiv); blogs 2026 | MEDIUM | extends. Against the real data a fit is not currently possible: the 689 legacy findings carry no numbers and no ground truth, the 142 shadow numbers carry no ground truth, and the E2 labelled packages carry no calibrator numbers (research/05 section 5); a fit needs numbers and labels on the same findings, so it waits for a run that produces both. Even then it holds only for a fixed model-prompt pair; because panel models change (fallback ladders, combo experiments), a fitted mapping goes stale, which argues against a numeric calibrator in the shared core until composition stabilises. |
| Practice descriptions: a confidence filter between review engine and comment publisher with category-specific thresholds; deterministic-rule findings pass unconditionally; suppressed findings logged to tune thresholds; adversarial review (proposer, challenger on a different vendor, arbiter) for false positives; a verification stack's false-negative rate is invisible unless a random sample of passing output is audited; thresholds drift permissive under one-sided pressure of visible false positives. | https://dev.to/dextralabs/how-to-build-a-custom-ai-code-review-agent-for-proprietary-codebases-329c; https://heym.run/blog/ai-code-review; https://sourcegraph.com/blog/automated-code-review-tools; https://hidekazu-konishi.com/entry/llm_output_verification_patterns.html `[S]` | 2026 | LOW to MEDIUM | supports calibration as a pluggable filter whose suppressed items are logged (the telemetry role); extends: a standing audit sample of passed or suppressed items. Practice description, not independent evidence. |
| Evidence gap: no controlled study of heterogeneous reviewer panels merged by a fuser for code or spec defect-finding; the closest are PoLL (correctness), the fuser paper (pairwise judging) and the code-evaluation bias paper. | web-03 section 6.5 | 2026-11-14 | HIGH (limits confidence) | extends: the panel's merge-and-grade design is an extrapolation; the project's own labelled packages are the real validation set. |

##### R1 5.3.5 Within-5.3 conflicts and gaps

| Conflict | Detail and which side is stronger |
|---|---|
| Panel versus best single judge | PoLL (2024, abstract primary, numbers secondary, correctness scoring, weaker judges) says a diverse panel beats one large judge. Nine Judges (May 2026, extracted, frontier models) says nine judges gave about 2 effective votes and the best single judge matched or beat the panel, noting PoLL compares with the average judge. Nine Judges is more recent and uses current-class models; PoLL is the better-known result. Neither is a defect-finding study; both files say to validate on own labelled data. |
| Single blind adjudicator versus panel | web-01 option 3 favours a blind, different-family adjudicator over debate; web-03 notes a single large judge is the setup PoLL argues against and recommends different-vendor judges, or at least two judges with reported agreement for offline scoring. Reconciling point: web-01's adjudicator makes a binary blocking decision, while web-03 advises against a required numeric per-finding calibrator; the two are compatible only if the adjudicator is binary and its true-negative rate is measured. |
| Verbalised confidence quality | Xiong 2024 (AUROC about 62.7%, overconfident), Tian 2023 (better calibrated than token probabilities) and Ferrer 2026 (best ECE 0.166 but AUC 0.668) disagree on whether it is "good". Common ground: top-skewed and weakly discriminative. Each uses 2023-2026 models; none tested the project's current model set. |
| Rubric as anchor | Rubric order bias (HIGH, extracted abstract) and a weak 2026 study (LOW) both say rubric text alone does not anchor; evidence gating is better supported. |
| Self-preference size | Panickssery (mechanism: recognition) versus the 2026 reanalysis (about 90% explained by uncertainty on hard items). Reconciled by recommending both blinding and a strong different-family judge. |
| Unverified or excluded | Verbosity figure from a June 2026 21-judge study (arXiv 2606.19544) attributed by a blog (https://digitortoise.com/mt-bench-explained) and the "always-A in 8 of 9 judges" figure were not confirmed against the primary paper and are excluded. The Apollo post date is unverified. |

##### R1 5.3.6 External-research options for who judges and calibration (from web-03 and web-01; options, not decisions)

| # | Option |
|---|---|
| 1 | Do not make a numeric per-finding calibrator a required role in the shared core; prefer reviewer agreement, the deterministic citation or evidence check and a binary blocking decision; keep the calibrator optional, disabled by default, logging raw outputs for later fitting. |
| 2 | If a calibrator or grader is kept: fresh context with the finding as external input; a different vendor, not only a different class; rubric option and criterion order permuted across a small number of runs; blinded input with opaque labels and no model, panel or combo names in schema or paths. |
| 3 | Treat the merge step as the fuser (reads all rationales, emits one decision); keep reflect's degrade rules (single-reviewer fallback, low convergence) as the fallback when diversity is missing. |
| 4 | Measure judge quality: a small fixed bias battery (swap order, pad length, rename author labels, rename files), blinded-versus-unblinded score differences in telemetry, E2 ground-truth packages as the labelled set; report the grader's true-negative rate on known-false blockers; compare the panel with its best single reviewer. |
| 5 | Keep a standing audit sample of findings the panel dropped or passed. |
| 6 | Re-derive any numeric threshold (such as the 0.82 or 0.85 values in the Reuse-Miss rule or the 0.80 convergence value) per model from logged data. |
| 7 | For an offline panel-scoring judge, use a different vendor from every reviewer in the scored panels, or at least two judges from different vendors with reported agreement. |
| 8 | Flag as open: validate on the project's own labelled data before treating any option as settled. |

#### R1 5.4 Finding location and fingerprinting across revisions

Source file: `research/web-04-finding-fingerprinting.md` (Tavily). Codebase context recorded there from research/03 and research/10: v1 `findings.cluster` and v2 `cluster_v2` use transitive O(n^2) union-find over a prose-harvested reference regex (misses `T01.02`, pulls `P1` from `D-P1`); replay of v1 found 195 chained rows and 83 mega-rows (up to 19 members over 8 sections); v2 flags chains but does not split them, and its section component is always empty so equal refs on one file merge at any distance (R1-D6); the quality figure (precision 21 of 25 = 0.84, n=25, on a 50-pair stratified sample; its recall is not a population recall) is AI-labelled, human labels pending; anchors over 200 characters are rejected (R1-D1); consumers need a location union (anchor, path plus line plus in_diff, file:section, multi-file).

##### R1 5.4.3 Transitive-chaining safeguards (union-find over-merge)

| Finding | Source | Date | Relevance | Relationship to codebase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Single linkage joins clusters when any pair is close, so chains of close intermediates merge distant members; complete linkage requires all pairs within the threshold and gives compact clusters but behaves badly with outliers. A record-linkage paper gives the minimal example (A-B and B-C close, A-C far) and a pipeline of blocking on stable fields, complete linkage inside each block, then a post-pass reassigning records by an attribute priority list. | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete-linkage_clustering; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4849582 (peer-reviewed); https://rich-d-wilkinson.github.io/MATH3030/7.3-hierarchical-clustering-methods.html | Dates not shown | HIGH | supports. This is R1-D6 (A-B on one anchor, B-C on another, 83 mega-rows) as a textbook failure. Complete-link admission (a candidate joins only if it matches every member or the representative) is affordable because clusters are small (reviewers x lenses). |
| Entity-resolution work: connected components ("partitioning") yields big clusters of dissimilar records and is the baseline other algorithms beat; Center assigns by similarity to the cluster centre, Merge-Center, Star and correlation clustering are alternatives; one paper measures closure at very high recall but 64% precision versus 97% precision (63% recall) for a pairwise classifier at threshold 0.65, and defines a "black hole threshold": if a component exceeds a size cap, raise the threshold and repartition. | http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol2/vldb09-1025.pdf (Hassanzadeh et al., VLDB 2009, peer-reviewed); https://www.cse.unr.edu/~hkardes/pdfs/organizationEntityResolution.pdf | 2009; second paper date not shown | HIGH | extends. Three cheap options: size cap with threshold escalation, centre-based assignment (v2 already computes a representative), pivot or correlation clustering. Our v2 pair precision 0.84 sits between 0.64 and 0.97, same direction only (different domain, AI-labelled). |
| One recent preprint reports that a hard size cap limits all chain paths at once (largest cluster 64 to 598 records with the cap off at equal F1; a cap too small, K=5, cut F1 from about 0.998 to 0.299). Image-text domain, read from a snippet only. | https://arxiv.org/html/2611.03080 (VL-Dedup) `[S][U]` | Nov 2026 | MEDIUM (reliability LOW to MEDIUM) | supports a size cap only as a safety net bounded below by the maximum legitimate cluster size (one finding per reviewer-lens run plus allowance); a cap below that silently splits true clusters. |

##### R1 5.4.4 Within-5.4 conflicts and gaps

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Hash on line content versus scope | CodeQL hashes a 100-character window of content (breaks on any edit in the window); Sonar hashes the first line; GitLab and SARIF prefer scope plus offset or logical location. The sources are complementary, not contradictory: content hash is exact, scope is drift-tolerant; web-04 recommends both components. |
| Cluster-by-location versus root cause | Practitioners merge different locations with the same root cause; mature trackers gate on location and rule. Web-04 resolves it by two levels (location cluster, then a root-cause group); the evidence for the second level is forum and blog only (LOW). |
| Codebase gap, not a contradiction | Every mature tracker gates matching on equal rule or category; the codebase key has no category gate (research/03, as stated in web-04). |
| Gaps | No published algorithm for clustering findings from several LLM reviewers; no measured over-merge or under-merge rates for that case; the preprint (VL-Dedup), forum and blog items and the `original_*` field names are not independently reproduced; some extracts returned excerpts rather than full pages. |

##### R1 5.4.5 External-research options for the location and clustering model (from web-04; options, not decisions)

| # | Option |
|---|---|
| R1 | One location model with explicit kinds (anchor, path plus line, file:section, whole-file, multi-file): a list of locations with normalised path or document id, optional line range, optional logical scope, optional quote hash, and revision; keep `in_diff` outside identity. |
| R2 | Identity as a versioned dictionary: category or rule, normalised path, logical scope, content hash, occurrence index kept outside the hash; compare on the greatest common version; never include reviewer-generated ids, run ids, timestamps or reviewer names. |
| R3 | Drift-tolerant text component: normalise whitespace and line endings, truncate to a fixed window, hash; this removes the R1-D1 rejection of long anchors; add a scope-based fallback component. |
| R4 | Tiered ordered matching gated on equal category: equal content hash, then same scope and same normalised claim, then overlapping ranges in one revision plus same defect shape; log a match reason per edge. |
| R5 | Never merge on an empty location component: require a content-derived component or keep a singleton. |
| R6 | Chaining safeguards, strongest to cheapest: complete-link or centre-based admission; black-hole threshold with a cap derived from reviewers x lenses plus allowance; keep v2's chain flag as a diagnostic; never set the cap below the maximum legitimate cluster size. |
| R7 | Cross-revision tracking as a separate link: store original revision and location, recompute current mapping, mark outdated rather than re-anchor, resolve renames first, then tiered matching between revisions; severity change must not split an identity. |
| R8 | Cross-reviewer matching on shared normalised fields only; keep (reviewer, model, lens) as run metadata; expose distinct-reviewer support and a deterministic representative tie-break. |
| R9 | A separate explicit "same root cause, different locations" link above location clusters; keep highest severity and the union of lenses on merge. |
| R1-R10 | Validate empirically before adopting any threshold: finish the human labelling and use the chain-split change (83 mega-rows before) as the acceptance metric. |

#### R1 5.5 External Research Summary

All of the following is external context. Where it differs from a verified code fact in research/01 to research/12, the code fact stands and the difference is recorded as a design choice or gap for the conflict log (synth-04). Owner scope is report only: nothing here is a roadmap or an implementation plan.

##### R1 5.5.1 Key takeaways and the design question each one informs

| # | Takeaway (external) | Informs | Evidence strength | Caveat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Union ("any reviewer flags") maximises recall and pays in false positives (82.7% recall, 85.0% FPR in one study); over-rejection by LLM reviewers is documented and richer prompts worsen it. | Merge and blocking rule: the any-member-blocks ledger rule (R1-C1) and the 65 versus 38 blocking result | HIGH direction, MEDIUM magnitude | Vulnerability and code domains, preprints, one number set from a snippet |
| 2 | Production systems separate finding from deciding: reviewers propose, a coordinator or verifier deduplicates, checks against source and applies a severity rubric before anything blocks. | Merge and blocking rule: candidate versus blocking split | MEDIUM (vendor first-party, no error rates) | No error rates published |
| 3 | A hard N-of-M quorum would discard real defects: 56.8% of confirmed defects were found by exactly one model; the second reviewer adds the most coverage (about 47% to 72%); LinkedIn verifies singletons while Cursor drops them. | Merge rule; PASS needing at least two valid reviewers; reflect single-reviewer DEGRADED versus ledger PASS-on-one (research/02, research/05) | LOW to MEDIUM (self-published corpus) | The reconciliation by reviewer independence is web-01's inference, not sourced |
| 4 | A panel of N is fewer than N votes (about 2 effective votes from nine judges); best single judge matched or beat the panel; diversity of labels is not independence. | Who judges; diversity gate (class versus vendor); telemetry comparing panel with best single reviewer | HIGH (extracted, May 2026) | NLI and preference tasks, not defect finding |
| 5 | Validators are agreeable (TPR above 96%, TNR below 25%); a missing vote must not default to an answer; thresholds need human-labelled calibration. | Blind grader true-negative rate; R1-D2/R1-D3 invalid-reviewer handling | HIGH (extracted) | Feedback-validity task; analogy only |
| 6 | Self-preference is real but partly judge uncertainty; blinding must cover panel identity (filename or label shifts scores); vendor diversity beats class diversity. | Who judges; calibrator diversity rule; the E2 combo-name leak in the judge schema | MEDIUM (mixed preprints; Claude-specific magnitudes unmeasured) | No direct proof that blinding improves a merged-report grader (evidence gap) |
| 7 | Verbalised numeric confidence is weakly discriminative and top-skewed; thresholds are not portable across models; fitted calibration goes stale. | Calibration: optional module, no required numeric calibrator in the shared core; the 0.80 and 0.82/0.85 constants | HIGH on weakness, mixed on best method | 2023-2026 models, none the project's current set |
| 8 | Rubric text alone does not anchor a judge (option order shifts scores); an evidence gate verified deterministically is better supported. | Calibration and grading rubric design | HIGH (order bias, abstract) / LOW (rubric-in-prompt study) | Domain mismatch |
| 9 | Every shipped scale keeps the middle severity tier distinct; collapsing the extremes was called "not ideal" by SonarQube staff; GitHub, CodeQL, Semgrep and GitLab keep severity, confidence and gating policy as separate things. | Severity scale: five tiers, `blocking` computed per consumer, card_convert collapse of `medium` and `important`, R1-D9 | HIGH (official docs) | Mapping table is the research agent's proposal; whether medium reflect drift blocks is an owner decision |
| 10 | Review-comment conventions model obligation as its own axis (blocking, non-blocking, if-minor); consequence-based tier definitions are the shared style. | Severity scale and blocking definition (three definitions today) | HIGH | Defaults differ between conventions |
| 11 | Identity should be a versioned dictionary (rule or category, normalised path, logical scope, content hash, occurrence index outside the hash); GitHub, Sonar, Semgrep, GitLab and DefectDojo all gate matching on rule or category; an empty location must never merge. | Location and clustering model: R1-D1 (anchor length), R1-D6 (empty-section over-merge), category gate | HIGH (official docs and source) | No published algorithm for LLM-reviewer findings |
| 12 | Transitive closure is the known-bad clustering baseline; complete-link or centre-based admission and a black-hole size cap are the documented remedies, the cap bounded below by the largest legitimate cluster. | Location and clustering model: R1-D6 mega-rows (83 before) | HIGH (VLDB, peer-reviewed) / MEDIUM (cap preprint, unverified) | Different domains; our precision figures are AI-labelled |
| 13 | Cross-revision tracking is a separate link from clustering: store original revision and location, recompute current, mark outdated, resolve renames first. | Location model across revisions and `in_diff` | HIGH (official docs) | `original_*` field names unverified against the live API |

##### R1 5.5.2 Contradictions and tensions across the four research files

| # | Between | Detail | Stronger evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | web-01 (Nine Judges) versus web-01 and web-03 (PoLL) | Panel beats single judge (2024, correctness scoring) versus best single judge matches or beats the panel (2026, frontier models) | Nine Judges: more recent, current-class models, extracted; both non-defect-finding. Validate on own labelled data. |
| 2 | web-01 option 3 (blind adjudicator) versus web-03 (single large judge is what PoLL argues against; no required numeric calibrator) | A single adjudicator versus panel pooling and calibrator scope | Unresolved by external evidence; compatible only with a binary adjudicator whose true-negative rate is measured and a different vendor from reviewers |
| 3 | Cursor (drop singletons) versus LinkedIn (verify singletons) versus Zenodo (most true defects are singletons) | Singleton handling | Zenodo is measured but LOW to MEDIUM; web-01's reconciliation by reviewer independence is an inference |
| 4 | Xiong 2024 versus Tian 2023 versus Ferrer 2026 | Whether verbalised confidence is "good" | None dominates; common ground is top-skewed and weakly discriminative |
| 5 | web-02: card_convert (`medium` to MINOR non-blocking) versus every vendor mapping reviewed | Collapse of the middle tier | Vendor docs agree across five tools; recorded as a design-choice conflict, not a code error |
| 6 | web-01 section on `confidence`: "computed but unused" versus research/02 R1-D4 | Display-only, not decision-bearing | research/02 (code-verified) |
| 7 | web-03: class-disjoint calibrator rule versus vendor-diversity evidence | Class diversity is weaker than vendor diversity (Apollo); the contract tracks vendor diversity but `calibrator_diversity: degraded` has no verdict effect | Codebase fact (research/05) plus Apollo (vendor blog, date unverified) |
| 8 | web-01 (Ellipsis evidence filter) versus research/02 R1-D5 | Our rule keeps an open blocking row when the anchor is absent from the document; the external filter drops unevidenced comments | Design-choice conflict; Ellipsis is a third-party summary (LOW to MEDIUM) |

|---|---|

##### R1 5.5.4 Evidence gaps that bound every option above

| Gap | Where reported |
|---|---|
| No external study of heterogeneous reviewer panels for defect-finding or specification and tasklist review | web-01 4.3, web-03 6.5 |
| No direct evidence that blinding improves accuracy for a merged-report grader | web-03 4.4 |
| No measured over-merge or under-merge error rate for clustering multi-LLM findings, nor its effect on blocking verdicts | web-01 4.3, web-04 |
| No validated algorithm for 3-to-5 severity mapping beyond vendor mappings | web-02 |
| All confidence-method studies use 2023-2026 models, none the project's current model set | web-03 |
| Our own precision and recall figures for clustering are AI-labelled; human labels pending | web-04 (from research/03) |

##### R1 5.5.5 Consolidated specific external-research options (all subject to codebase verification and owner decision)

| # | Option | Section |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Make a finding blocking only after verification against source (anchor and citation checks, then an independent binary adjudicator from a different vendor); keep the any-reviewer set as the candidate filter only. | 5.1.5 option 1, 5.3.6 option 2 |
| 2 | Use reviewer overlap to route and prioritise verification; do not use a hard quorum as the only gate. | 5.1.5 option 2 |
| 3 | Count an invalid or truncated reviewer block as an abstention; a PASS needs at least two valid reviewers (web-01 inference; would change the assertion at tests/review/test_review_ledger.py:385 on purpose). | 5.1.5 option 3 |
| 4 | Five-tier core severity with SARIF `level` and `rank` as export, `blocking` computed per consumer, consequence-defined tiers, native severity preserved, versioned alias table. | 5.2.5 |
| 5 | Optional, disabled-by-default calibrator; fresh context, different vendor, permuted rubric order, blinded input with no panel or combo names; measure the grader's true-negative rate and compare the panel with its best single reviewer. | 5.3.6 |
| 6 | Versioned identity dictionary with a category gate and no merge on an empty location; complete-link or centre-based admission with a size cap bounded below by reviewers x lenses; separate cross-revision tracking link; separate root-cause link. | 5.4.5 |
| 7 | State the verdict bias, log blockers dropped at verification per round, keep an audit sample of dropped or passed findings, and track outcome (findings upheld or fixed), not volume. | 5.1.5, 5.3.6 |
